title: Levi's Priesthood and the Seven Tablets
sum: Jacob is back at Bethel, where he made his vow (Genesis 28). Levi dreams that he is made a priest of God Most High. Jacob pays his vow: a tenth of everything, people and animals, gold and clothing. Counting his sons upward from the unborn Benjamin, he finds that Levi is the tenth, the Lord's portion, and dresses him as a priest. Levi offers the sacrifices of the Feast of Booths, and the angel explains the law of the second tithe, eaten each year before the Lord at the chosen place.

When Jacob plans to make Bethel a lasting sanctuary, God renames him Israel and an angel brings seven tablets: Jacob reads the future of his family, and is told that Bethel is not the place. He keeps an eighth day of the feast, then Deborah dies, Benjamin is born on the road, and Rachel dies and is buried near Bethlehem.
readings: Read as the founding of the priesthood

Genesis has no priest in Jacob's family. Jubilees makes Levi a priest at Bethel, before Aaron and before Sinai, and grounds the priests' tithes in Jacob's vow. The point is that the priesthood of the writer's own day is as old as Israel.
Read as a lesson about the one sanctuary
Jacob may sacrifice at Bethel but may not build a temple there. The law of Deuteronomy 12 and 14, the one place God chooses for his name, is already in force, and Bethel is not that place.

views.E: Read as Scripture, the chapter shows God's order for priesthood and tithe given long before Sinai and kept by Jacob. The tablets Jacob reads, and the book he writes, belong to the line of revealed writings handed down through Levi (45:16).
views.H: Scholars read the chapter as a defense of the priests and their income in the Second Temple period: the tenth son, the tithe of herds, the second tithe eaten in the sanctuary. Charles saw in "priest of God Most High" the title of the Hasmonean priest-kings. The ban on a sanctuary at Bethel keeps worship at the one chosen place.
views.N: Hebrews 7 argues from the same chapters of Genesis but in the other direction: Levi, still "in his father's body," paid tithes to Melchizedek through Abraham (Hebrews 7:9–10), so Melchizedek's priesthood is greater than Levi's. Jubilees gives Levi Melchizedek's title. Jesus' promise in John 14:26 that the Spirit will bring all he said to mind is close to the angel's promise in 32:25.
views.J: The Testament of Levi tells Levi's dream at Bethel; Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer knows Levi as Jacob's tenth son given to God (Charles notes it). Jews of the Second Temple kept more than one tithe; Tobit 1:7 speaks of a "second tenth" spent in Jerusalem, as here.
views.W: Read as an early Jewish witness rather than as Scripture, the chapter shows how Jews of the 100s BC read Genesis 28–35: as the history of their own institutions. Measured by the 66 books, the priesthood is given at Sinai, to Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:41), not to Levi at Bethel.

deep.h: The tenth son and the second tithe
deep.b:
Jubilees joins two tithes. First, Jacob gives a tenth of all he brought from Haran, and the tenth son, Levi, falls to God (32:2–3). Then he gives "a tenth again," which the angel explains as the second tithe: grain, wine and oil eaten by the worshiper before the Lord at the chosen place, each year's crop before the next harvest, with any leftovers burned (32:10–14). The tithe of cattle and sheep goes to the priests (32:15).

The law of Moses has a tithe for the Levites (Numbers 18:21–26), a tithe eaten at the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 14:22–26), and a third-year tithe for the poor (Deuteronomy 14:28–29). Jews later debated whether these were one tithe or several. Jubilees, like Tobit 1:7, counts at least two, and says they were written on the heavenly tablets before Moses.

Genesis 28:22 promised that Jacob's stone would "become a house of God." Jubilees lets Jacob build an altar and keep the whole feast there, but an angel forbids a lasting sanctuary: "this is not the place" (32:22). Readers who knew Israel's history remembered Jeroboam's calf at Bethel (1 Kings 12:29). Jubilees closes that door at the very beginning: there is to be one sanctuary, in the place God will choose.

echoes: Genesis 14:18–20; Genesis 28:18–22; Genesis 35:1–20; Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Leviticus 23:33–43; Numbers 29:12–38; Hebrews 7:4–10; John 14:26; Jeremiah 31:15

settings.by: a dream given to Levi (the text does not say who appoints him)
settings.when: the night Jacob stays at Bethel
settings.why: To show Levi made priest of God Most High, him and his sons forever, before Sinai; the next verses carry it out (32:3; 32:9).
settings.readers: Priests of the Second Temple, who traced their line to Levi. Charles notes that "priest of the Most High God" was the title chosen by the Maccabean priest-kings.

settings.what: The law of the second tithe and the herd tithe
settings.by: the angel of the presence, citing the heavenly tablets
settings.to: Moses on Sinai, and through him all Israel
settings.when: told after Jacob pays his vow at Bethel
settings.why: To bind every Israelite household to bring a second tenth of grain, wine and oil each year to the chosen place and eat it there before the Lord, and to give the tithe of herds and flocks to the priests. It answers the question of what Jacob's "tenth again" meant, and fixes the time limit: one year.
settings.readers: Jews of the Second Temple who brought tithes to Jerusalem and argued about how many tithes the law required. Tobit 1:7 describes a pious man doing what this law says.

settings.what: God renames Jacob and promises the earth
settings.when: after Jacob plans to build up Bethel
settings.why: To confirm the promise of Genesis 35:10–12, but widened: kings, and rule over all nations under heaven.
settings.readers: Jews of the 100s BC (the date on the book's audience card), a small people under foreign kings, who hear the promise of kings from Jacob (Genesis 35:11) widened to rule over every nation under heaven (32:18–19).

settings.what: The seven tablets and the angel's orders
settings.to: Jacob, in a vision of the night
settings.when: a night in the seventh month, the month of the Feast of Booths (32:4; 32:16)
settings.why: To show Jacob his family's future, forbid a lasting sanctuary at Bethel, send him to Isaac, foretell his death in Egypt and burial at home, and order him to write it all down.
settings.readers: Readers who held that Israel's priests kept books from the fathers (45:16). Origen later quotes a Prayer of Joseph in which Jacob says he read the tablets of heaven (Charles).

title: Reuben, Bilhah and the Law Revealed in Full
sum: While Jacob and Leah visit Isaac, Reuben sees Bilhah bathing, goes to her at night while she sleeps, and lies with her. She wakes, cries out and he flees; she tells no one, but when Jacob comes she says she is no longer clean for him. Jacob never comes near her again.

The angel then speaks to Moses. The law against lying with a father's wife is on the heavenly tablets, its penalty is death by stoning, and there is no atonement for it. Why then did Reuben live? Because the law had not yet been revealed in full: it is revealed now, in Moses' days, for all generations. The chapter ends with Jacob's family settling near Isaac and Rebekah at Abraham's house.
readings: Read as the answer to a question

Genesis 35:22 tells Reuben's sin in one line and Genesis 49:4 punishes it only by loss of rank. Jubilees asks why the law of Leviticus 20:11 was not applied, and answers: the law was not yet revealed in full.
Read as a warning to the writer's people
The story serves the law: there is "no greater sin" than sexual sin in a people meant to be "a kingdom of priests" (33:20). What was overlooked once will not be overlooked again.

views.E: Read as Scripture, the chapter shows God's law already written in heaven and revealed in stages, with full knowledge given to Moses. Bilhah is shown as wronged, not guilty.
views.H: The book's method is clear here: a short, awkward verse of Genesis becomes a story and then a law, with the patriarch's lack of punishment explained by a theory of gradual revelation. The law ends by calling Israel a holy nation and a kingdom of priests (33:20; compare Exodus 19:6).
views.N: Charles compared 33:16 with Paul: "transgression does not exist where there is no law" (Romans 4:15) and "with no law there, sin is not counted" (Romans 5:13). Paul and Jubilees both see the law as revealed at a point in history, but they draw opposite conclusions: for Jubilees the law is eternal and binding; for Paul it was "added on account of transgressions, until the offspring would come" (Galatians 3:19).
views.J: The Mishnah agrees that the penalty is stoning (Sanhedrin 7:4). But some rabbis denied that Reuben sinned at all: "Anyone who says that Reuben sinned with Bilhah is nothing other than mistaken"; he only moved his father's bed (Talmud, Shabbat 55b). The same page records other sages who said he did sin.
views.W: Read as a witness rather than as Scripture, the chapter is an early answer to a question Genesis leaves open: why the patriarchs were not judged by the law of Moses. Genesis records the act (Genesis 35:22) and its cost to Reuben (Genesis 49:4). Christians have their own answers to that question; see the topic Law of Moses.

deep.h: Why Reuben was not put to death
deep.b:
The question was real for ancient readers. The law says that a man who lies with his father's wife and the woman "must be put to death" (Leviticus 20:11), and Deuteronomy curses him (Deuteronomy 27:20). Yet Reuben lived, kept his place among the twelve tribes, and lost only the firstborn's rank (Genesis 49:3–4; 1 Chronicles 5:1).

Jubilees answers in 33:15–16: until Moses, "the ordinance, the judgment and the law had not been revealed in full for everyone." The law existed on the heavenly tablets, but its full form and penalty were not yet given. So the angel adds a warning: "Let no one say" that Reuben's case is a precedent (33:15).

Other answers: some rabbis said Reuben only disturbed his father's bed (Talmud, Shabbat 55b). Paul makes a related point about sin before the law (Romans 5:13–14), but for a different purpose.

echoes: Genesis 35:21–26; Genesis 49:3–4; 1 Chronicles 5:1; Leviticus 18:8; Leviticus 20:11; Deuteronomy 22:30; Deuteronomy 27:20; Exodus 19:6; Deuteronomy 10:17; Romans 4:15; Romans 5:13; 1 John 5:16

settings.what: Bilhah tells Jacob what Reuben did
settings.why: To tell the wrong done to her while she slept, so that Jacob knows why she is unclean for him. The blame falls on Reuben.
settings.readers: Readers who knew Genesis 35:22, where Jacob only hears of the act. The book lets Bilhah speak, and the law that follows (33:10–20) judges the deed.

settings.what: The law against lying with a father's wife
settings.by: the angel of the presence, citing the heavenly tablets
settings.to: Moses on Sinai, who is told to command and write it for Israel
settings.when: after the story of Reuben and Bilhah
settings.why: It binds every man in Israel, and the woman too: no man may lie with his father's wife; both are to be stoned the day they do it, with no atonement. It answers the objection that Reuben lived and was forgiven, by saying the law was not yet fully revealed in his day. Its purpose is to keep a holy, priestly nation free of uncleanness.
settings.readers: Jews of the 100s BC for whom purity in marriage marked Israel off from the nations. The Mishnah later lists the same sin among those punished by stoning (Sanhedrin 7:4).

title: The Amorite War, Joseph Sold, and the Day of Atonement
sum: Seven Amorite kings ambush Jacob's sons near Shechem. Jacob, at home with the grieving Isaac, marches out with six thousand men, kills six of the kings, takes back his herds, puts the rest under tribute and builds two towns. This is the war Jacob speaks of in Genesis 48:22.

A year later Jacob sends Joseph to his brothers. They plot, then sell him to traders bound for Egypt, and send Jacob his robe dipped in a goat's blood on the tenth of the seventh month. Jacob mourns; Bilhah and Dinah die in the same month. That, the angel says, is why Israel fasts and makes atonement with a goat on the tenth of the seventh month every year. The chapter ends with the names of the brothers' wives.
readings: Read as history filled in
Genesis 48:22 mentions land taken "from the Amorites with my sword and my bow," and Leviticus 16 sets the date of the fast. Jubilees supplies the war and the event that the fast remembers.
Read as a book of its own time
Charles saw the Amorite war as an old legend retold with the place names of the Maccabean wars, so that Jacob's victory foreshadows the victories of the writer's own people.

views.E: Read as Scripture, the chapter gives the origin of the Day of Atonement: a fast of repentance first kept in memory of the brothers' sin and Jacob's grief. The fast becomes a yearly call to grieve for sin and be cleansed.
views.H: Two aims stand out. The Amorite war recasts Genesis 48:22 and an older legend (the Testament of Judah 3–7) with names like Tappuah, Hazor, Beth-horon and Timnath, places of the Maccabean campaigns (Charles). The Day of Atonement is given a patriarchal origin, as the book does for every feast.
views.N: Hebrews reads the yearly Day of Atonement as a reminder of sins that only Christ's one sacrifice removes (Hebrews 9:7–12; 10:3).
views.J: Charles notes that the rabbis knew nothing of this origin of the Day of Atonement. The Mishnah teaches that the Day atones for sins against God, but for sins against another person only after he is appeased (Yoma 8:9), a rule that fits a fast born of a wrong done to a father.
views.W: Measured by the 66 books, the Day of Atonement comes from Leviticus 16, and Hebrews reads it in the light of Christ's one sacrifice (Hebrews 9:7–12). Jubilees' story of its origin is an early Jewish explanation that the 66 books do not give.

deep.h: Joseph sold and the Day of Atonement
deep.b:
Leviticus 16 orders the fast of the tenth day of the seventh month but tells no event behind it. Jubilees supplies one. The brothers send the robe dipped in a goat's blood to Jacob "on the tenth of the seventh month" (34:12); Jacob mourns all night and for a year. "That is why" Israel is to afflict itself on that day and make atonement with a young goat, once a year, "for they had grieved their father's tender love for his son Joseph" (34:18).

Three things stand out. The sin remembered is a sin of brothers against a brother and a father. The goat of the lie becomes the goat of atonement (see the note on 34:18). And the day is for grief: "grieve for their sins ... and cleanse themselves" (34:19). Leviticus also speaks of humbling oneself and being cleansed (Leviticus 16:29–31), but Jubilees adds the memory of a family's wrong.

Genesis 34 has Simeon and Levi attack Shechem against Jacob's will. Genesis 48:22 has Jacob say he took land from the Amorites "with my sword and my bow." Jubilees tells this second story: seven kings, Jacob's six thousand men, six kings killed, tribute laid on the rest. Charles found the same legend, more fully, in the Testament of Judah 3–7 and in medieval Hebrew retellings, and identified most of the kings' towns with places of the Maccabean wars (see the note on 34:4).

echoes: Genesis 48:22; Genesis 34; Genesis 37:12–36; Genesis 41:45; Genesis 46:10; Leviticus 16:29–34; Leviticus 23:26–32; Hebrews 9:7–12; Hebrews 10:3; 1 Maccabees 9:50

settings.when: the evening of the tenth of the seventh month (34:12–13), and the year after
settings.why: His words follow Genesis 37:33–35. The day his grief began becomes the date of the Day of Atonement (34:18).
settings.readers: Israelites who kept the fast of the tenth of the seventh month (Leviticus 16:29) learn here why they grieve on that day (34:18–19).

settings.what: The law of the Day of Atonement
settings.to: Moses on Sinai, for all Israel
settings.when: after the story of Joseph's sale
settings.why: It binds all Israel to fast on the tenth day of the seventh month, once a year, and make atonement with a young goat for their sins. It explains why the day exists: the sin of Jacob's sons against their father and brother. Its purpose is to make the fast a yearly time of grief for sin and cleansing.
settings.readers: Jews of the Second Temple who kept the Day of Atonement at the Temple. The Qumran movement, which kept copies of Jubilees, held to the book's 364-day calendar, so for them this date fell on the same day of the week every year (see 6:32 and the book's opening pages).

title: Rebekah's Last Request
sum: In the first year of the forty-fifth jubilee Rebekah tells Jacob to honor his father and brother, and tells him she has seen in a dream that she will die this year, aged 155. Jacob laughs; she is still strong. She asks Isaac to make Esau swear not to harm Jacob. Isaac answers that Esau's ways are violent and that he now loves Jacob more, but that Jacob's guardian is greater than Esau's.

Then Rebekah makes Esau promise to bury her near Sarah and to love his brother. Esau swears, and says he knows Jacob will be king over him. Jacob promises the same before Esau's eyes. That night, after a meal with her sons, Rebekah dies, and both sons bury her in the double cave.
readings: Read as a farewell
Genesis gives Rebekah no death scene. Jubilees gives her the last words of a matriarch, as it gives testaments to Abraham and Isaac.
Read as the setting for chapters 37–38
Esau's oath here is the one he will break. The reader is told in advance that if he attacks Jacob he will fall into Jacob's hands (35:16).

views.E: Read as Scripture, Rebekah is a model of a godly mother who foresees her death and settles peace in her family. Isaac's word that "Jacob's guardian is great, mighty and honored" (35:17) is an assurance of God's protection for the righteous.
views.H: Scholars note the book's sharp contrast of the brothers: Jacob "blameless and upright," Esau violent and led astray by foreign wives. The contrast fits a time of conflict between Judea and Idumea (Edom).
views.N: Isaac's reversal, now loving Jacob more than Esau, matches the prophets' "Jacob I loved. But Esau I hated" (Malachi 1:2–3), which Paul quotes about God's free choosing (Romans 9:13). Charles saw in "Jacob's guardian" the earliest clear mention of a guardian angel, the belief behind Matthew 18:10 and Acts 12:15.
views.J: George Syncellus quotes this scene in Greek, though he gives it to Josephus (Charles). In Syncellus' short form, Isaac himself exhorts the brothers and foretells that Esau will fall into Jacob's hands.
views.W: Read as a witness rather than as Scripture, the chapter is an early Jewish meditation on brotherly love and sworn oaths, and it shows how much darker Esau's picture is here (35:9–15) than in Genesis 33.

echoes: Genesis 25:22–28; Genesis 26:34–35; Genesis 27:29; Genesis 27:40; Genesis 49:31; Exodus 20:12; Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:13; Matthew 18:10; Acts 12:15

settings.when: the first year of the forty-fifth jubilee, the year of her death
settings.why: To bind Jacob to honor his father and brother all his life, and to prepare him for her death.
settings.readers: Readers who knew the command to honor father and mother (Exodus 20:12): the book shows Jacob keeping it before Sinai, and promising to honor his brother too (35:4).

settings.what: Rebekah's request to Isaac, and his answer
settings.why: Rebekah wants an oath from Esau to protect Jacob. Isaac's answer judges Esau and reassures her that Jacob is protected by a greater guardian.
settings.readers: Jews of the 100s BC (the date on the book's audience card), who lived beside Edom (Idumea). The chapter's dark picture of Esau prepares the war of 37–38, whose ending Charles tied to John Hyrcanus, by whom Edom was made tributary.

settings.why: To bind both sons to love each other. Esau's oath, sworn to his mother, is the oath he breaks in 37:13.
settings.readers: The same readers, for whom the oath Esau swears here (35:24) is the measure of his guilt when he breaks it (37:13). A book that holds Israel to sworn law makes a broken oath the cause of the war.

title: Isaac's Testament and Death
sum: Isaac calls his two sons, tells them he is going "the way of my fathers," and asks to be buried with Abraham. His last words are a testament: do what is right, love your brothers as your own souls, reject idols, remember the God of Abraham. He makes them swear by the great Name never to plan evil against each other, and warns that whoever does will fall into his brother's hand, be blotted out of the book and burned like Sodom.

He divides his goods, the larger share to the firstborn; Esau says the birthright is Jacob's. Isaac blesses them both and dies glad, at 180. Esau goes to Seir, Jacob stays at Abraham's tower near Hebron. Five years later Leah dies, and Jacob mourns the wife he came to love.
readings: Read as a testament
Like Abraham's farewell speeches (20–22), Isaac's is a sermon: brotherly love, faithfulness to God, and warning. The reader knows Esau will break it.
Read as a story of reconciliation that fails
For one day the brothers are "of one mind" (36:17). The next chapter shows how short that peace was.

views.E: Read as Scripture, Isaac's testament teaches love of brother, rejection of idols and fear of God's name, and the end of the righteous patriarch, who dies in peace.
views.H: Scholars read the oath and curse as preparing the war of 37–38, so that Jacob's killing of Esau is shown as just: Esau breaks a sworn oath by God's name. The praise of Leah and the burial details fit the book's care for the matriarchs. The testament form, a dying father's moral charge, is shared with the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, a related work, which also has the phrase "slept the eternal sleep" (36:18; Charles).
views.N: Isaac's "love your brothers as a man loves his own soul" echoes Leviticus 19:18, which Jesus called the second command (Matthew 22:39). The books of life and destruction (36:10) stand behind the New Testament's "book of life" (Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:12). Jesus' word against oaths (Matthew 5:34) sets a different course from Isaac's great oath.
views.W: Read as a witness rather than as Scripture, Isaac's testament is moral teaching from Second Temple Judaism, close to the command of brotherly love in Leviticus 19:18, which Jesus called the second command (Matthew 22:39).

echoes: Genesis 35:27–29; Genesis 49:29–33; Genesis 50:5; Genesis 18:19; Leviticus 19:18; Exodus 32:32–33; Genesis 19:24; Ecclesiastes 12:5; Matthew 5:33–37; Revelation 20:12

settings.when: the sixth year of the week, the day of his death
settings.why: To leave his sons a charge of righteousness and brotherly love, and to bind them by an oath on God's name, with a curse on whoever plans evil against his brother. It is meant to prevent the war that follows, and it explains why Esau's death is just.
settings.readers: Readers who knew the farewell of a dying father as a form: Jacob's in Genesis 49, and the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, which share this chapter's phrase "slept the eternal sleep" (36:18; Charles).

settings.what: Isaac divides his goods and blesses his sons
settings.why: To settle the inheritance in peace: the firstborn's larger share goes to Jacob, with Esau's consent.
settings.readers: Readers who knew Genesis 25:29–34 and 27, where the birthright passes by a sale and a trick. Here Esau gives it up before his father (36:14), so Jacob's line holds it by consent.

title: Esau Breaks His Oath
sum: When Isaac dies, Esau's sons learn that Jacob received the birthright and turn on their father: why let the younger have it? Esau tells them he sold it and was tricked, and that he has sworn peace. They refuse, threaten him, and hire soldiers from Aram, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, the Horites and the Kittim. Forced to lead them, Esau remembers his old hatred and forgets his oath.

While Jacob mourns Leah at the tower near Hebron, four thousand men surround it. Jacob shuts the gates and speaks to Esau from the wall: is this the oath you swore? Esau answers with sayings: when the boar changes its skin, the wolf makes peace with the lamb and the raven turns white, then he will make peace. Seeing that Esau means to kill him, Jacob orders his men to attack.
readings: Read as the end of Esau's story

Genesis leaves Esau in Seir, at peace with Jacob. Jubilees ends his story with a broken oath and a war he started. Charles thought this an old legend, kept also in the Testament of Judah and later Hebrew retellings.
Read as a mirror of Judea and Edom
Esau's army gathers the enemies of Judea in the writer's day, and the war ends with Edom serving Jacob, as Idumea was made subject under John Hyrcanus (38:8, 38:14).

views.E: Read as Scripture, the chapter shows the fate of one who swears by God and breaks his word, and God's protection of the righteous, who seek peace until there is no choice.
views.H: Charles saw the war of 37–38 as an ancient legend recast to fit the Hasmonean wars against the Idumeans. The book makes Esau's sons, not Esau, the first movers (37:2–11), and makes Jacob the one who seeks peace. Genesis knows nothing of it.
views.N: Esau's sayings use the pictures of Isaiah 11:6–7, the wolf with the lamb and the lion like the ox, to say peace will never come. For the New Testament's picture of hostility ended, compare Ephesians 2:14–17. Hebrews 12:16–17 also remembers Esau, who "sold his own birthright" and later sought the blessing in vain.
views.J: Charles quotes the Yalkut Shimoni and the Chronicles of Jerahmeel, which tell the same attack during the mourning for Leah, with four thousand men around the tower. In those versions Esau himself is more to blame.
views.W: Measured by Genesis, the brothers' quarrel ends in reconciliation (Genesis 33:4) and a shared burial of Isaac (Genesis 35:29). Read as a witness rather than as Scripture, this chapter is a later legend, and it shows the hostility between Jews and Edomites in the writer's age.

deep.h: A war the Bible does not tell
deep.b:
Genesis gives the twins a reconciliation: "Esau ran to meet him, hugged him, fell on his neck and kissed him, and they wept" (Genesis 33:4). They bury Isaac together (Genesis 35:29), and Esau moves to Seir because the land cannot hold both their herds (Genesis 36:6–8). The law later commands, "Do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother" (Deuteronomy 23:7).

Jubilees tells instead a war in which Jacob kills Esau. The book prepares for it carefully: Rebekah and Isaac warn that Esau will fall into Jacob's hand (35:16; 36:9), Esau swears peace twice (35:24; 37:4), and he is forced by his sons before his hatred returns (37:11–13). Jacob shuts his gates and argues before he fights. The story justifies the war by the oath. Charles found the legend in older form in the Testament of Judah 9 and later forms in medieval Hebrew collections, and dated its final shape to the Hasmonean wars with Idumea.

echoes: Genesis 25:29–34; Genesis 27:30–41; Genesis 33:4; Genesis 36:6–8; Deuteronomy 2:4–5; Deuteronomy 23:7; Isaiah 11:6–7; Jeremiah 13:23; Hebrews 12:16–17; Obadiah 10

settings.why: To show that the war began with Esau's sons, who would not accept the birthright's loss, and that Esau at first refused.
settings.readers: Jews of the 100s BC (the date on the book's audience card), who knew Edom (Idumea) as a near enemy. Charles linked Aduram, where Esau is buried (38:9), to Adora, one of the Idumean towns John Hyrcanus captured.

settings.by: Jacob from the tower wall, then Esau
settings.to: each other, in front of Esau's army
settings.when: as Esau's army surrounds the tower, during the mourning for Leah
settings.why: Jacob names the broken oath; Esau answers that peace between them is as impossible as a white raven. The exchange shows that Jacob sought peace and Esau chose war.
settings.readers: Readers who knew Isaiah's picture of the wolf with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6) hear Esau use it to say that peace will never come (37:21).

title: The Death of Esau and the Kings of Edom
sum: Judah urges his father to shoot, since the sons will not kill their own uncle. Jacob's first arrow kills Esau, his second kills Aduran the Aramean. Jacob's sons and their servants go out from the four sides of the tower and rout the army; four of Esau's sons flee to Seir. Jacob buries Esau where he fell.

Pressed hard in Seir, Esau's sons submit. Jacob tells his sons to make peace, and they lay a yoke of tribute on Edom, which it paid until Jacob went down to Egypt and which, the angel says, it has not escaped "to this day." The chapter ends with the list of Edom's kings from Genesis 36.
readings: Read as fulfillment
Everything foretold comes true: Esau falls into Jacob's hand (35:16; 36:9), Edom serves Jacob (Genesis 27:40), and the elder serves the younger (Genesis 25:23).
Read as a claim about the present
"To this day" speaks to the writer's own readers: Edom's subjection is old and lawful. Charles linked it to John Hyrcanus' conquest of Idumea.

views.E: Read as Scripture, the chapter shows God's judgment on a broken oath and the fulfillment of Isaac's blessing that Esau would serve his brother.
views.H: Charles dated the book by this chapter: Aduram is Adora, an Idumean town that Josephus says John Hyrcanus took when he subdued the Idumeans (Antiquities 13.9.1). Others date the book earlier and see an older legend reused. Either way, Edom's yoke "to this day" is aimed at the writer's own time.
views.N: The New Testament does not tell this war. Romans 9:12–13 uses "the elder will serve the younger" and "Esau I hated" about God's choosing, not about war.
views.J: Later Jewish tradition gave Esau's death to Hushim son of Dan, at Jacob's burial (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 50:13; Sotah 13a; Charles notes both). The Yalkut tells the sortie from the four sides of the tower exactly as here (Charles).
views.W: Measured by Genesis, Edom's kings (Genesis 36:31–39) are a record of its early rulers, and Genesis tells no war between the brothers. Read as a witness rather than as Scripture, the chapter shows how Jews of the 100s BC saw Edom.

echoes: Genesis 25:23; Genesis 27:40; Genesis 36:31–39; Genesis 46:9; 2 Samuel 8:14; 2 Kings 8:20–22; Numbers 24:18; Obadiah 18–21; Romans 9:12–13

settings.why: To urge Jacob to fight, and to explain why the sons will not kill their uncle themselves: he is their father's equal, held in honor.
settings.readers: Readers who honored Judah as the tribe of kings (Genesis 49:10): here Judah speaks first, and in 38:5 he leads the sortie.

settings.by: the angel, quoting the record of Genesis 36
settings.when: after the account of Edom's subjection
settings.why: To complete the history of Esau's line, and to show Edom's kings ruling a people already bound to serve Jacob.
settings.readers: Charles linked the chapter's "to this day" (38:14) to John Hyrcanus, by whom Edom was finally made tributary to Israel.
